In this exercise you will practise the difference between **attributes** and **aesthetics**.

By the end, you should be able to:

- set fixed visual properties such as point size or transparency,
- map variables to visual properties using `aes()`,
- decide when an extra aesthetic helps or overloads the plot.

## Load packages and data

We will use data from @blomkvist2017reference. Keep this `.Rmd` file and the `data` folder together so the relative path below works when you run chunks or knit the document.


```{r}
# Load tidyverse, including ggplot2 and read_csv().
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
# Load the data.
blomkvist <- read_csv("data/blomkvist.csv")

# Remove rows where smoker status or hand reaction time is missing.
blomkvist <- drop_na(blomkvist, smoker, rt_hand_d)
```

```{r}
# Inspect the variables before plotting.
glimpse(blomkvist)
```

## Start with a simple plot

Create a scatterplot with age on the x-axis and dominant-hand reaction time on the y-axis.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  geom_point()
```

## Attributes: fixed visual properties

Attributes are fixed settings. They do not depend on a variable in the data.

Complete the code so that all points are smaller and partly transparent.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(size = ___, alpha = ___)
```

Now set all points to the same colour. This is still an attribute because the colour is fixed.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6, colour = "___")
```

## Aesthetics: visual properties mapped to variables

Aesthetics are mappings from variables to visual properties. They go inside `aes()`.

Map `smoker` to colour.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d, colour = ___)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)",
       y = "Dominant-hand reaction time (ms)",
       colour = "Smoking status")
```

What does colour make easier to compare?

Write one sentence here: ___

## Redundant coding for accessibility

Sometimes using two aesthetics for the same grouping variable is helpful. For example, colour and shape can make groups easier to distinguish when printed in greyscale.

Map `smoker` to both colour and shape.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist,
       mapping = aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d,
                     colour = ___, shape = ___)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)",
       y = "Dominant-hand reaction time (ms)",
       colour = "Smoking status",
       shape = "Smoking status")
```

Does the plot still feel readable? Why or why not?

## A warning example: size for categories

It is technically possible to map an unordered category to size, but it is usually a poor choice because size suggests quantity or importance.

Run the code and compare it with the colour/shape plot above.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist,
       mapping = aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d, size = smoker)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)",
       y = "Dominant-hand reaction time (ms)",
       size = "Smoking status")
```

Why is size a weaker choice for smoker status?

Write one sentence here: ___

## Common mistake: fixed values inside `aes()`

A fixed colour should usually be set outside `aes()`. Run these two plots and compare them.

```{r}
# Fixed colour outside aes(): all points are blue and no colour legend is needed.
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(colour = "blue", alpha = 0.6)
```

```{r}
# Fixed text inside aes(): ggplot treats "blue" like a data category.
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"), alpha = 0.6)
```

Why does the second plot create a legend?

Write one sentence here: ___

## Add a trend line carefully

Use colour for smoker status and add one linear trend line per group. Keep the points transparent so they do not dominate the plot.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist,
       mapping = aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d, colour = ___)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.45) +
  stat_smooth(method = "___", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)",
       y = "Dominant-hand reaction time (ms)",
       colour = "Smoking status")
```

## Global and layer-specific mappings

Where you put `aes()` matters. In the first plot below, `colour = smoker` is a global mapping, so it applies to all layers.

```{r}
# Colour applies to both points and trend lines.
ggplot(data = blomkvist,
       mapping = aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d, colour = smoker)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

In the second plot, `colour = smoker` is only inside `stat_smooth()`, so it applies only to that layer.

```{r}
# Colour applies only to the trend lines.
ggplot(data = blomkvist,
       mapping = aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45) +
  stat_smooth(mapping = aes(colour = ___), method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

What changes between the two plots?
